spinach.history: Spinach spread west from Asia. Its tender leaves became a familiar spring and autumn crop.
facts: Young leaves are often smoother.
Some varieties have crinkled leaves.
The stalk can lengthen as flowering begins.
spinach.tips: Thin crowded seedlings and check soil moisture before watering.

rocket.history: Rocket has long been grown around the Mediterranean. The leaves are used both fresh and cooked.
facts: The leaves can be deeply lobed.
The flavour is often peppery.
The pale flowers have dark veins.
rocket.tips: Keep the bed evenly moist and cut tender leaves without pulling the crown.

parsley.history: Parsley has a long history in Mediterranean cooking. Flat and curly forms are both cultivated.
facts: Flat leaves have broad lobes.
Curly leaves have ruffled edges.
New leaves emerge from the centre.
parsley.tips: Keep the seedbed moist while seedlings establish and cut outer leaves first.

dill.history: Dill has long been grown as an aromatic herb. Both the foliage and the dried fruits are used in cooking.
facts: Its leaves are finely divided.
Flowers cluster at the stem tips.
The hollow stalk is easily crushed.
dill.tips: Sow where it will grow and handle the stems gently at harvest.

coriander.history: Coriander has been grown since antiquity. Its fresh leaves and dry fruits serve different roles in cooking.
facts: Lower leaves are broad and lobed.
Upper leaves are finer.
The dried fruits are round.
coriander.tips: Sow in cool conditions and separate flowering stems from leaf bunches.

chicory.history: Chicory has long been gathered and cultivated in Europe. Leaf forms are still used in cooked greens and salads.
facts: Basal leaves form a rosette.
Many forms have bitter leaves.
Open flowers are often blue.
chicory.tips: Pick the outer leaves of the recorded crop and leave the centre intact.

endive.history: Endive is a long-established salad green. Broad-leaved and curly forms are grown for different dishes.
facts: Curly forms have narrow fringed leaves.
Broad forms have wider leaves.
The centre may be paler than the outside.
endive.tips: Handle the loose head gently and remove damaged outer leaves.

chard.history: Chard belongs to the same species as beet. Growers selected it for leaves and stalks instead of the swollen root.
facts: Stalks can be pale or coloured.
Leaf blades can be smooth or puckered.
New leaves emerge from the crown.
chard.tips: Cut mature outer leaves without damaging the inner growth.

onion.history: Onions have a long cultivation history. Green onions are gathered for their leaves and immature base.
facts: The leaves are hollow.
The white base is formed by overlapping sheaths.
Bruised leaves lose their shape quickly.
onion.tips: Lift gently and keep the leaves aligned in clean bunches.

leek.history: Leeks have long been cultivated in European gardens. The pale stem is valued for its mild flavour.
facts: The leaves are flat.
Overlapping leaf sheaths form the pale shaft.
The leaf tips spread into a fan.
leek.tips: Lift the whole plant with care and keep soil out of the leaf folds.

vlita.history: Amaranths have been used as leafy vegetables in many regions. In Greece the cooked greens are often called vlita.
facts: The leaves grow along upright stems.
Tender tips are used in cooked greens.
Mature stalks become fibrous.
vlita.tips: Pick tender growth from the recorded crop and keep it shaded after cutting.

kaukalithra.history: Kaukalithra is a Greek name used for aromatic greens in traditional cooking. Local names alone do not establish the identity of a plant.
facts: Farm records tie a name to a harvest.
Tender stems are easily crushed.
Aromatic greens are often mixed after sorting.
kaukalithra.tips: Handle only the grower's recorded crop and keep batches separate.

cabbage.history: Leaf cabbages belong to a crop group cultivated for many generations. Different forms have been grown for leaves and heads.
facts: Leaf surfaces can look waxy.
Midribs are often prominent.
Outer leaves surround new growth.
cabbage.tips: Support broad leaves during cutting and keep damaged leaves separate.

myroni.history: Myroni is a Greek name used for fragrant greens in traditional kitchens. Its identity should come from the farm record.
facts: Local names can differ.
Finely cut leaves bruise readily.
Small bunches are easier to sort.
myroni.tips: Handle only the recorded crop and place it loosely in a clean crate.

beet.history: Beet crops with edible leaves predate many modern root varieties. Root beets and chard belong to the same species.
facts: The leaves grow from a rosette.
Some stalks have red veins.
The root can be round or elongated.
beet.tips: Lift roots gently and avoid damaging the leaves if they will be used.

radish.history: Radish has long been cultivated for its pungent root. Growers selected many shapes and colours.
facts: Leaves often feel rough.
Roots vary in shape and colour.
The root can become spongy as it ages.
radish.tips: Check roots regularly and lift them gently when well formed.

celery.history: Celery was grown as an aromatic plant before thick-stalked forms became widespread. Leaf celery is valued for its scented foliage.
facts: Leaf stalks are ribbed.
Leaves have divided leaflets.
The aroma is released when leaves are bruised.
celery.tips: Handle the stalks gently and keep sorted bunches in the shade.
